newsitem.title: INDIA: Cricket-Indian punters betting on almost anything.
newsitem.headline: Cricket-Indian punters betting on almost anything.

text.p: The name of the game is betting. Cricket is just an excuse.

Cricket, India's national obsession, has given rise to a huge illegal betting business worth millions of dollars in which the adrenaline of a wager has become more important than the joys of the game, punters and bookies say.

But the seamier side of what is called a gentleman's game showed up this year when former Indian test cricketer Manoj Prabhakar accused an unnamed colleague of offering him a huge amount to help fix a match.
While an inquiry is investigating the yet-unsubstantiated charge, what is certain is that bookies have a field-day whenever a one-day game is on.
"You can call me a compulsive gambler. In one-day cricket every ball provides a different possibility," punter Rajiv Mehta, a businessman by profession, told Reuters."
"I'd rather bet on cricket than buy lottery tickets. When cricket is not on I usually bet on snooker, golf and even hockey," he said.
For most punters, placing money on cricketing events is one way of blending their gambling instinct with the nation-wide love for the game.
Most punters bet on results but many bet on guessing top scorers, top wicket takers or the best batsman of a series. Some even bet on whether a toss-winning team will bat first or not, a punter said.

"For some it might be a way of making quick money but that has its pitfalls," corporate executive Ashwin Patel said. "I don't understand racing and horses don't excite me. Cricket is a good alternative."
Punters have spotted an array of betting possibilities -- tosses, sixes, boundaries, batting partnerships, run rates during slog overs, victory margins. The list is long.
Old-fashioned five-day test matches only lure a few punters. Most are driven now by limited-over games.

Unlike in Britain and some other parts of the world, authorised bookmakers do not exist in India, where betting is illegal. But the illegal betting business is fairly organised, bookies and punters say.
Communications were once a problem. The arrival of mobile telephones and the ease with which long-distance calls can now be made in India has made things easier for organised betting.
"Not everybody deals in millions. Small bets are common. It all happens by word of mouth," said a bookie, who did not want to be identified.
"Sometimes, when matches have been hit during the rainy season, we have cancelled all bets and returned the money. I don't remember any bookie I know who has not paid up," he told Reuters.

Unsubstantiated rumours of players being in league with bookies were long ignored, but Prabhakar's column in the weekly Outlook magazine this year prompted India's cricket authorities to order a probe.

Prabhakar accused his unnamed team-mate of offering him money to sabotage a match against Pakistan three years ago. The charge raised questions about how two players from a team of 11 could fix a match.

"Sponsors and bookies have started exerting pressure and the games are now being increasingly fixed," Prabhakar said in the magazine, which also reported that some sports journalists helped bookies by acting as informants.

"I fail to understand how one or two players can be bribed to change the course of the match. Even if one player gets involved, others can come good and turn the match around," former Indian captain Kapil Dev said in an interview before Prabhakar dropped the match-fixing bombshell.
Former Indian team manager Ajit Wadekar has also contested rumours about match-fixing.

"I had the telephones of the players' rooms tapped without their knowledge for about a month after the disastrous tour of South Africa (in 1992) when rumours were afloat in the media about match-fixing," Wadekar said. "I found absolutely nothing incriminating or objectionable."
The Board of Control for Cricket in India has asked a former chief justice of India's Supreme Court, Y.V. Chandrachud, to inquire into allegations of match-fixing.
The inquiry has no statutory authority but the multi-million dollar illegal betting business will come under intense scrutiny if any names are divulged.
